## Today's questions

- How does an area describe the probability of an interval?
- How do we calculate and simulate normal probabilities?
- How can a continuous model approximate discrete vote counts?
- How does a distribution of possible partners become a payoff distribution?

We will read integrals as accumulated areas and use geometry or R to
calculate them.

**Reading:** PSD Chapter 4, Sections 4.1-4.4.2.

## Probability mass and probability density

Last week, a PMF assigned probability to each possible value:

$$p_X(x)=P(X=x),\qquad \sum_x p_X(x)=1.$$

For today's continuous models, a **density** allocates probability
over intervals:

$$P(a<X\le b)=\text{area under }f_X\text{ between }a\text{ and }b.$$

The random variable still maps outcomes to numbers. We change how we
describe its distribution.

## A uniform waiting-time model

Suppose an outreach worker arrives after $T\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,10)$
minutes. All intervals of the same length inside $[0,10]$ have equal probability.

```{r}
#| label: uniform-figure
#| echo: false
uniform_area()
```

$$P(2\le T\le5)=(5-2)(0.1)=0.3.$$

## Why point probabilities are not enough

Suppose each exact time in our uniform $[0,10]$ model had probability $c>0$.

For $N$ distinct times,

$$P(T\in\{t_1,\ldots,t_N\})=Nc.$$

We can choose more than $1/c$ distinct times. That would give a
probability greater than one.

Each exact time has probability zero. The whole interval has probability one:

$$P(T=t)=0,\qquad P(0\le T\le10)=1.$$

The point probabilities alone lose the distribution's information.
The density preserves how probability spreads across intervals.

## Reading an integral

$$P(a<X\le b)=\int_a^b f_X(x)\,dx.$$

The bounds identify the interval. The density supplies the height.

Imagine dividing the interval into thin rectangles:

$$\text{probability}\ \approx\ \sum_i f_X(x_i)\,\Delta x.$$

The integral is the limit as those rectangles become arbitrarily thin.

For the uniform example, the rectangles all have height $0.1$.

## A sloping density

A different model has $f_T(t)=t/50$ on $[0,10]$, zero elsewhere.

```{r}
#| label: triangle-figure
#| echo: false
triangle_area()
```

The shaded trapezoid has area
$(5-2)(0.04+0.10)/2=0.21$. No antiderivative is needed.

## What makes a valid density?

$$f_X(x)\ge0,\qquad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_X(x)\,dx=1.$$

A uniform wait between 0 and 10 **minutes** has density $0.1$ per minute.

Measure that same wait in **hours**. Its range is $[0,1/6]$ and its
density is $6$ per hour.

$$P(T\le3\text{ minutes})=3(0.1)=0.05(6)=0.3.$$

Density can exceed one. Area is a probability and stays between zero and one.

## The CDF still answers the same question

$$F_X(x)=P(X\le x).$$

For a density model,

$$F_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x} f_X(t)\,dt,\qquad
P(a<X\le b)=F_X(b)-F_X(a).$$

The CDF accumulates area from the left. Where it is differentiable,
its slope is the density: $F_X'(x)=f_X(x)$.

For continuous density models, including or excluding the endpoints
does not change an interval's probability.

## A uniform CDF

```{r}
#| label: uniform-cdf-figure
#| echo: false
uniform_cdf()
```

Here $F_T(t)=t/10$ within $[0,10]$, with 0 to the left and 1 to the right.

$$P(2<T\le5)=F_T(5)-F_T(2)=0.5-0.2=0.3.$$

## Narrow intervals and a single point

For $T\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,10)$ minutes, zoom in around 5 minutes:

| Interval | Width (minutes) | Probability | Probability / width |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| $[4.5,5.5]$ | 1 | 0.1 | 0.1 per minute |
| $[4.9,5.1]$ | 0.2 | 0.02 | 0.1 per minute |
| $[4.99,5.01]$ | 0.02 | 0.002 | 0.1 per minute |

The interval's **probability** shrinks toward zero. Its probability
**per unit of width** stays at $0.1$ per minute.

For a smooth density and a narrow interval,

$$P(x-\epsilon\le X\le x+\epsilon)\approx 2\epsilon f_X(x).$$

Width times density gives probability, just as time times speed gives distance.

## Density at a point is a local rate

Where the density is continuous at $x$,

$$f_X(x)=\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}
\frac{P(x-\epsilon\le X\le x+\epsilon)}{2\epsilon}.$$

Divide probability by interval width, then shrink the interval.
The limit gives a rate at $x$, with no particular interval left to specify.

Some authors write $p(x)$ for this density. Here we use $f_X(x)$.
That notation does not turn density into $P(X=x)$.

| R expression | Result | Meaning |
|---|---:|---|
| `dunif(5, 0, 10)` | 0.1 | Density at 5, per minute |
| `punif(5, 0, 10)` | 0.5 | Probability $P(T\le5)$ |

`punif()` includes an implicit interval: everything at or below its argument.

## Four useful R prefixes

| Question | Uniform example | Normal example |
|---|---|---|
| Density height at $x$ | `dunif(x, 0, 10)` | `dnorm(x, mu, sigma)` |
| Probability at or below $x$ | `punif(x, 0, 10)` | `pnorm(x, mu, sigma)` |
| Value at cumulative probability $p$ | `qunif(p, 0, 10)` | `qnorm(p, mu, sigma)` |
| Simulated values | `runif(N, 0, 10)` | `rnorm(N, mu, sigma)` |

For a discrete distribution, `d` gives **mass**. For a continuous
distribution, `d` gives **density**.

## Simulation checks an area calculation

```{r}
#| label: uniform-code
set.seed(93001)
waits <- runif(50000, min = 0, max = 10)
mean(waits >= 2 & waits <= 5)
punif(5, 0, 10) - punif(2, 0, 10)
```

One draw is one waiting time. The logical comparison identifies draws
inside the interval.

**Demo 1:** Change the number of repetitions. The underlying probability
stays at $0.3$. Demo 2 optionally checks the sloping-density example.

## Expectation as a weighted average

$$E[X]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x f_X(x)\,dx.$$

This is the continuous counterpart of $\sum_x x p_X(x)$.

Small intervals have approximate weight $f_X(x)\Delta x$.
Multiply each representative value by its weight, then add.

For $T\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,10)$, symmetry gives $E[T]=5$ minutes.

**Question:** Does every density have its mean at the middle of its support?

## Variance measures variation in outcomes

$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[(X-\mu)^2]=E[X^2]-\mu^2.$$

The formulas and interpretation carry over from discrete random variables.

For $T\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,10)$,

$$E[T]=5,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(T)=\frac{100}{12}\approx8.33,
\qquad \operatorname{SD}(T)\approx2.89.$$

Variance uses minutes squared. SD uses minutes.

More simulated waits improve our estimate of this variance. They do not
make the model's waiting times less variable.

## Transformations and expectation

The rules for fixed constants still hold:

$$E[aX+b]=aE[X]+b,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X).$$

For a general transformation $g$, average its values over the distribution:

$$E[g(X)]=\int g(x)f_X(x)\,dx.$$

For example, $E[T^2]=100/3$, whereas $(E[T])^2=25$.

The two calculations answer different questions.

## A finite population of potential partners

Four people have minimum acceptable payments of **5, 15, 15, and 45** points.
Choose one person uniformly at random.

| Minimum payment $c$ | 5 | 15 | 45 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| $P(C=c)$ | $1/4$ | $1/2$ | $1/4$ |
| $F_C(c)$ | $1/4$ | $3/4$ | $1$ |

The average minimum payment is $E[C]=20$.

Each person has equal probability. The three distinct payment values do not.

## Expected payoff and the mean partner

An 80-point project succeeds when your offer $a$ meets the partner's minimum.

$$Y_a=\begin{cases}80-a,&C\le a,\\0,&C>a.\end{cases}$$

At an offer of 15, the four possible earnings are $65,65,65,0$.

$$E[Y_{15}]=48.75.$$

A hypothetical partner with the **mean** minimum of 20 rejects that offer,
giving a payoff of zero.

The threshold transformation cannot generally be applied after averaging.

## Crossing payoff CDFs

```{r}
#| label: crossing-figure
#| echo: false
payoff_cdfs()
```

Offer 15 has the higher mean. Offer 45 is more likely to exceed 20 points.
Only offer 15 can exceed 50 points.

**Demo 8:** Read the tail probability as $P(Y>y)=1-F_Y(y)$.

We have connected density, cumulative probability, and moments.

After the break: the normal model, election forecasts, and a discrete
vote-count approximation.

## The normal model

$$X\sim\operatorname{Norm}(\mu,\sigma),\qquad
E[X]=\mu,\quad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.$$

Following PSD, the second parameter is the **standard deviation**.

$$f_X(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}
\exp\left[-\frac12\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2\right].$$

This formula defines the curve. We use `dnorm()` to draw it and
`pnorm()` to calculate its accumulated area.

No hand evaluation of a normal integral is required.

## Location and spread

```{r}
#| label: normal-shapes-figure
#| echo: false
normal_shapes()
```

Changing $\mu$ shifts the center. Increasing $\sigma$ spreads the same
total area over a wider range and lowers the peak.

## Standardization

If $X\sim\operatorname{Norm}(\mu,\sigma)$, then

$$Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\sim\operatorname{Norm}(0,1).$$

$Z$ measures distance from the mean in standard deviations.

$$P(X\le x)=P\left(Z\le\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right).$$

We can use `pnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)` directly, or standardize
first and use `pnorm((x - mu) / sigma)`.

## The normal model's central areas

| Distance from the mean | Probability |
|---|---:|
| Within one SD | About 68% |
| Within two SDs | About 95% |
| Within three SDs | About 99.7% |

For example,

$$P(\mu-\sigma\le X\le\mu+\sigma)
=P(-1\le Z\le1)\approx0.683.$$

These percentages describe the normal model. They are not universal
rules for every distribution.

## A hypothetical election forecast

Suppose the final margin follows $V\sim\operatorname{Norm}(3,5)$,
in percentage points.

```{r}
#| label: normal-win-figure
#| echo: false
normal_area()
```

The shaded area is $P(V>0)$, the probability of victory in this model.
The parameters are assumptions, not estimates we fit today.

## A normal density and its CDF

For $V\sim\operatorname{Norm}(3,5)$, $F_V(x)=P(V\le x)$.

```{r}
#| label: normal-pdf-cdf-figure
#| echo: false
normal_pdf_cdf()
```

The shaded **area** on the left equals the **height** on the right:
$F_V(0)\approx0.274$. The win probability is $1-F_V(0)\approx0.726$.

The CDF rises fastest where the density is highest.

## Win probabilities and close elections

```{r}
#| label: normal-probabilities
pnorm(0, mean = 3, sd = 5, lower.tail = FALSE)
pnorm(1, mean = 3, sd = 5) - pnorm(-1, mean = 3, sd = 5)
```

The first expression gives $P(V>0)$.
The second gives $P(-1\le V\le1)$.

Write the event and its CDF expression before choosing the R command.

**Demo 3:** Compare these areas with `dnorm(0, 3, 5)`.

## The forecast mean and the chance of victory

Hold the SD at 5 and the victory threshold at zero. Vary the assumed mean $\mu$:

$$P(V>0)=\Phi(\mu/5),\qquad \Phi(z)=P(Z\le z),\quad Z\sim\operatorname{Norm}(0,1).$$

```{r}
#| label: normal-win-curve-figure
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.7
normal_win_curve()
```

Here the horizontal axis changes the **mean of the distribution**.
The previous CDF moved a **threshold within one fixed distribution**.

## Density at a tie

For this model, $f_V(0)\approx0.06664$ per percentage point.

| $\epsilon$ (pp) | Interval width | $P(-\epsilon\le V\le\epsilon)$ |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.5 | 1.00 | 0.066574 |
| 0.1 | 0.20 | 0.013328 |
| 0.01 | 0.02 | 0.001333 |

For narrow intervals, probability is approximately
**width times density**.

As the width shrinks, the probability tends to zero. Its ratio to the
width tends to $f_V(0)$.

## Quantiles run the CDF backward

Start at a cumulative probability, move across to the curve, then down
to its margin threshold.

```{r}
#| label: normal-quantile-cdf-figure
#| echo: false
normal_quantile_cdf()
```

`qnorm(c(.10, .90), mean = 3, sd = 5)` gives $-3.41$ and $9.41$.
These enclose the middle **80%** of future margins under this model.

## A central forecast interval

```{r}
#| label: central-figure
#| echo: false
normal_central()
```

The endpoints are approximately $-3.41$ and $9.41$ percentage points.
The total area outside is $0.20$, divided equally between the tails.

This describes the **random final margin**, given the model, rather than
a confidence interval for an unknown mean.

## Simulating the forecast

```{r}
#| label: normal-sim-code
set.seed(93004)
v <- rnorm(50000, mean = 3, sd = 5)
c(win = mean(v > 0), mean = mean(v), variance = var(v))
```

**Demo 4:** Compare CDF calculations and model moments with the simulation.

The number of draws controls simulation accuracy.
The supplied $\sigma=5$ controls variation across possible election margins.

## A continuous margin and a discrete payoff

A hypothetical contract costs \$1.50 and pays \$2 for a victory:

$$W=\begin{cases}2,&V>0,\\0,&V\le0,\end{cases}
\qquad Z=W-1.50.$$

Let $p=P(V>0)$. Then

| Net profit $z$ | $-1.50$ | $0.50$ |
|---|---:|---:|
| $P(Z=z)$ | $1-p$ | $p$ |

The margin $V$ is continuous in the model. The payout and profit are discrete.

## A likely profit and an expected profit

For the contract,

$$E[Z]=2p-1.50,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Z)=4p(1-p).$$

Here $p\approx0.726$, so the probability of profit exceeds one half,
but expected profit is about **minus five cents**.

The loss is three times the size of the gain.

**Demo 6:** Transform each simulated margin into its corresponding payout.
Changing a fixed price shifts the mean profit, leaving variance unchanged.

## A discrete election model

Exactly 200 voters choose A or B independently.
Each chooses A with probability $p=0.5$.

$$K=\text{votes for A}\sim\operatorname{Binom}(200,0.5).$$

$$E[K]=100,\qquad \operatorname{SD}(K)=\sqrt{50}\approx7.07.$$

$K$ is a count. A tie, $K=100$, has positive probability.

These independence and common-probability assumptions define a toy model.

## A normal approximation to the count

```{r}
#| label: binomial-figure
#| echo: false
binomial_overlay()
```

Match the binomial mean and SD with
$K^*\sim\operatorname{Norm}(100,\sqrt{50})$.

Each displayed binomial bar has width one vote and area $P(K=k)$.

## An exact tie becomes an interval

```{r}
#| label: continuity-figure
#| echo: false
binomial_overlay(tie=TRUE)
```

$$P(K=100)\approx P(99.5<K^*<100.5).$$

The half-vote boundaries form a **continuity correction**.
They assign the mass at 100 to its surrounding unit-width bin.

## Exact and approximate election probabilities

```{r}
#| label: continuity-code
sd_count <- sqrt(200 * .5 * .5)
dbinom(100, size = 200, prob = .5)
pnorm(100.5, 100, sd_count) - pnorm(99.5, 100, sd_count)
```

Both are about $0.0564$.

A **strict victory** is $K\ge101$, approximated by $K^*>100.5$.
It has probability about $0.4718$, not $0.5$.

**Demo 5:** Compare exact probabilities, the approximation, and simulated counts.

## Counts and percentage-point margins

In a two-candidate election with $n$ votes,

$$V=100\left(\frac{K}{n}-\frac{n-K}{n}\right)
=\frac{200K}{n}-100.$$

A one-vote increment changes the margin by $200/n$ percentage points.

The tie bin in margin units is $(-100/n,100/n)$.
For $n=200$, that is $(-0.5,0.5)$ percentage points.

Probabilities agree across units when we transform both the interval and
the distribution.

## Assumptions behind the approximation

- Independent Bernoulli votes with a common $p$ give a binomial count.
- Independent votes with different $p_i$ give a Poisson-binomial count.
- Dependence between votes can change the count's variance and shape.

A normal approximation works best when the count has enough variation
and neither boundary is too close to its center.

Next week: a fuller account of why sums often have approximately normal
distributions.

## A forecast has additional sources of uncertainty

The binomial example assumes a known $p$ and a fixed electorate size.

A forecast may also represent uncertainty about support, turnout,
or shared errors.

B2 supplies a hypothetical normal margin model directly.
Its parameters do not come from a specified binomial electorate.

The count example explains how a continuous approximation can assign zero
probability to a point even when the discrete event has positive probability.

## B2 programming: values and their weights

```{r}
#| label: population-code
costs <- c(5, 15, 15, 45)
values <- sort(unique(costs))
counts <- as.numeric(table(factor(costs, levels = values)))
probability <- counts / length(costs)
data.frame(values, probability, cdf = cumsum(probability))
```

**Demo 7:** Compute moments by probability weights and by all four people.

For this finite population, use
`mean((costs - mean(costs))^2)` for variance.

## B2 programming: a loop over decisions

For each offer, calculate its payoff against every possible partner.

```{r}
#| eval: false
for (i in seq_len(nrow(result))) {
  offer <- result$offer[i]
  payoff <- ifelse(costs <= offer, budget - offer, 0)
  result$expected[i] <- mean(payoff)
  result$variance[i] <- mean((payoff - mean(payoff))^2)
}
```

**Demo 9** supplies the complete function and result table.
Row 1 corresponds to offer 0, so the row index differs from the offer.

This loop calculates exact finite-population quantities. Random sampling
with replacement provides a separate simulation check.

5. Which differences reflect simulation error rather than model uncertainty?
